title: Fire Arrows and Funeral Boats: Did Vikings Really Do That?
summary:
In movies and TV shows, it's a classic scene: a dead Viking is placed on a boat that drifts out to sea, and an archer shoots a fiery arrow to set it ablaze. You've seen it in the 1958 film "The Vikings," the History Channel's "Vikings," and even "Game of Thrones." But did the Vikings actually do this? Experts say probably not.

"From an archaeological standpoint, we have no evidence for this very common motif," Erin McGuire, an anthropology professor at the University of Victoria in Canada, told Live Science. She noted that it would be hard to differentiate a fire set by a fire arrow from a regular fire. Also, shipwrecks with human remains are "very, very rare globally," she added. "It takes particular kinds of environmental conditions for them to be preserved and I know of none from the Viking Age."

However, the Vikings did burn ships. McGuire said there are archaeological examples of ships burned during funerary practices while still on land and then buried. These include the ninth-century Myklebust ship, found in a burial mound in Norway and built for a rich person, possibly a king.

The closest historical evidence comes from Ahmad ibn Fadlan, a 10th-century Arab traveler who visited Viking groups along the Volga River. In his account, a Viking chieftain is placed on a boat that is set ablaze. But there are key differences: no flaming arrow was used — a chief mourner lit the fire — and the boat was on land, not water.

Experts also doubt it was even possible. "My own experiments show that it is not at all easy to set something alight with flaming arrows," said Matthias Toplak, head of archaeology at the Viking Museum Haithabu in Germany. He noted that cremation requires high heat for hours, and at sea the ship would likely sink before the body burned. Plus, a burning boat could drift into other ships or harbor facilities.

"However romantic the idea of such a funeral scene may be, I unfortunately consider it highly unlikely," Toplak said. Howard Williams, an archaeology professor at the University of Chester, suspects the trope comes from the 1958 film "The Vikings."
why_it_matters: This is a case study in how entertainment can invent a 'fact' that millions accept, and in how researchers test popular stories against physical evidence — a skill that matters whenever students meet confident claims online, in films or in textbooks.

background_read: Ship burials really did happen — but on land. In Norway, the Oseberg and Gokstad ships were buried in mounds with treasures for the dead, and in England an Anglo-Saxon ship grave at Sutton Hoo was dug into the ground rather than sent out to sea. Norse mythology also features a famous burning ship: in the medieval Icelandic texts that preserve Norse stories, the god Baldr's body is laid on a ship and set alight. That scene, more than any real funeral, probably fed the modern image.

Ahmad ibn Fadlan (a 10th-century Arab diplomat who travelled up the Volga River — the long river running through Russia — and wrote down what he saw) left one of the few eyewitness descriptions of a Viking chieftain's funeral, and even his account describes a boat burned on land, lit by a mourner rather than an arrow.

The film "The Vikings" (1958, starring Kirk Douglas and Tony Curtis) put the flaming-arrow version in front of millions of viewers, and later TV series copied it. Meanwhile, today's researchers — such as Erin McGuire of the University of Victoria in Canada and Howard Williams of the University of Chester in England — study how such stories travel from old texts and films into what people believe happened in the past.

OPEN QUESTION: how do films and TV shape what we believe about history?

perspectives.perspective: Positive / what the myth gives us
perspectives.description: Films and shows have made the Vikings one of the most recognisable cultures in history, and that fascination fills museums, books and classrooms. The myth is also partly rooted in real practice: Scandinavians genuinely burned ships as part of funerals, just on land and in graves.

Critics argue that the flaming-arrow scene buries the more interesting evidence — buried ships, grave goods, and a 10th-century Arab traveller's eyewitness account. It also makes the past look like pure spectacle, when archaeology shows rituals that were careful, expensive and highly organised.

perspectives.perspective: Analytical / why the evidence is thin
perspectives.description: Archaeologists face a preservation problem: organic material such as wood and human remains survives only in unusual conditions, so the absence of a shipwreck burial is not proof that none existed. That uncertainty is exactly why researchers lean on experiment and written sources instead of trusting famous images.

New excavation techniques — soil chemistry, isotope analysis, better dating — could reveal traces of burned or buried vessels that older methods missed. Researchers also hope clearer public communication will let audiences enjoy Viking stories while knowing which parts come from evidence and which come from Hollywood.
